title: Corrosion behavior of polar marine steel FH40 in simulated marine environments
content: With the increasing strategic value of the Arctic Passage, corrosion behavior of polar marine steel in harsh environments has become a key issue for ship life-cycle reliability. This work systematically compares the corrosion behavior of FH40 polar marine low-temperature steel under three conditions: 20 °C immersion, 20 °C salt spray, and −60 °C immersion. Combined with EBSD characterization, the effects of environmental factors on the corrosion mechanism, product evolution, grain boundary characteristics, and dislocation density are elucidated. Results show that the corrosion mechanism is synergistically controlled by environment and temperature. Immersion at 20 °C is dominated by uniform dissolution with local pitting, while −60 °C immersion presents typical local pitting. In contrast, 20 °C salt spray exhibits crater-like morphology with internal accumulation and deep edge erosion, resulting from dry–wet cycling and Cl− enrichment. EBSD analysis indicates that all samples are dominated by high-angle grain boundaries (HAGB). The salt spray sample shows the highest HAGB fraction (69.4%) and the highest grain-boundary density (0.42 µm−1), together with the smallest average grain size (7.11 µm), consistent with its highest corrosion rate. Electrochemical tests confirm that corrosion products provide no protective effect; instead, they accelerate substrate corrosion by forming oxygen concentration cells. Although the rust layer of the salt spray sample is approximately 3–4 times thicker than that of the immersion sample, its weight loss and corrosion rates are correspondingly 3–4 times higher, indicating no positive correlation between rust layer thickness and protective performance. Low temperature significantly inhibits corrosion kinetics. Compared with 20 °C, the corrosion rate and rust layer thickness at −60 °C decrease by approximately one order of magnitude, and grain boundary structure and dislocation density remain at low levels. This work addresses a critical knowledge gap in comparative study of immersion and salt spray corrosion of low-temperature marine steel, providing a basis for service life prediction and protective design of polar marine vessels.
